claims.text: The initial refractory high-entropy alloy has a random solid-solution microstructure.
Tungsten-based or MoNbTaTiW refractory high-entropy alloys can be used as intermediate layers in plasma-facing components.
A tailored heat-treatment or alloying procedure can induce stepwise, controllable coherent nanoprecipitation in the refractory high-entropy alloy.
The induced coherent nanoprecipitates may be silicide or carbide phases.
The proposed benefit will hold during operation from approximately 800 °C to 1000 °C under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
The nanoprecipitates form coherent, clean, well-bonded interfaces with the matrix.
Coherent nanoprecipitates act as conduits for enhanced phonon transport.
The nanoprecipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Coherent precipitate interfaces facilitate phonon transmission and create additional continuous heat-conduction pathways.
Impeding dislocation movement with the precipitates reinforces the matrix.
Controlled coherent nanoprecipitation can produce a favorable combination of strength and tensile ductility in a tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy.
The treated alloy will retain or marginally enhance strength and ductility under 800–1000 °C cyclic service conditions.
The treatment will increase effective thermal conductivity by roughly tens of percent relative to an unmodified intermediate layer.
Current high-entropy-alloy intermediate layers have comparatively low thermal conductivity.
Excessive nanoprecipitate volume fraction or size can compromise ductility.
Departures from the target heat-treatment window can cause unwanted phase transformations.
Operation beyond 1000 °C or radiation damage may limit the treatment's effectiveness.
